meta.description: Max Planck never said it. The chauffeur joke is Jewish folklore traced to 1926; Charlie Munger told a Planck version in 2003 and called it apocryphal.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Your question is quite simple. Hence, I'm going to ask my chauffeur to respond'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Max Planck: an old folk joke that has starred a rabbi, Einstein and von Braun. Charlie Munger told the Planck version and called it apocryphal.

answer.label: Not Max Planck — an old folk joke
answer.authorDates: Jewish folk anecdote · earliest version located by Quote Investigator: 1926
answer.sourceLine: Planck never said it, and nothing suggests the lecture swap ever happened. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke to Jewish folklore. Its earliest match is Jacob Richman’s Laughs from Jewish Lore (1926), where the hero is Rabbi Ezekiel Landau of Prague. Planck took the starring role in later retellings, such as Charlie Munger’s 2003 talk, and Munger called the story apocryphal ↗ as he told it.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: Jacob Richman · Funk & Wagnalls, New York, 1926
Rabbi Ezekiel Landau of Prague (not a scientist)
Charlie Munger, UC Santa Barbara lecture, October 3, 2003 (published in Poor Charlie’s Almanack)

source.excerpt: By the way, there’s a famous story about Max Planck that is apocryphal: After he won his prize, he was invited to lecture everywhere, and he had this chauffeur who drove him around to give public lectures all through Germany. And the chauffeur memorized the lecture, so one day he said, “Gee, Professor Planck, why don’t you let me try it by switching places?” So he got up and gave the lecture. At the end of it, some physicist stood up and posed a question of extreme difficulty. But the chauffeur was up to it. “Well,” he said, “I’m surprised that a citizen of an advanced city like Munich is asking so elementary a question, so I’m going to ask my chauffeur to respond.”
trail: 1926 — Jacob Richman’s Laughs from Jewish Lore ↗ prints “Even His Driver Was a Scholar.” Rabbi Ezekiel Landau trades places with his driver. When the fake rabbi gets a hard question, he says: “You have asked me a very, very silly question. Even my driver can answer that.”

1948–1998 — The hero keeps changing, as Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows: the Preacher of Dubno (1948), an unnamed “well-known atomic scientist” (1958), Albert Einstein (Reader’s Digest, January 1978), Wernher von Braun (1987) and a bishop-theologian (1998).

2003 — Charlie Munger tells the story about Max Planck in a UC Santa Barbara lecture and calls it “apocryphal.” He retold it at USC’s law school commencement on May 13, 2007. Both talks are in Poor Charlie’s Almanack ↗.
2023 — Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that the anecdote “originated within Jewish folklore,” that a version was circulating by 1926, and that the creator of the original tale is unknown.
source.excerptNote: This is Munger’s telling from his 2003 UC Santa Barbara lecture, as printed in Poor Charlie’s Almanack ↗. Even here, the man telling the Planck version calls it apocryphal. The popular line “Your question is quite simple. Hence, I’m going to ask my chauffeur to respond” is the heading of Quote Investigator’s article. It is the researcher’s summary, and no historical source uses those exact words.

Munger’s own telling appears in Poor Charlie’s Almanack, a modern book that is still in copyright. The 1926 Richman joke book uses different words and was published before 1931.

author.name: Charlie Munger
author.kicker: The man who made it famous — but didn’t write it
author.heading: The investor who kept telling the Planck version
author.metaLine: 1924–2023 · Investor, vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
author.bio: Charlie Munger was Warren Buffett’s longtime partner and vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. He told the chauffeur story about Max Planck in a 2003 talk at UC Santa Barbara and again at USC’s law school commencement in 2007, saying he “frequently” told it. Both times he called it apocryphal. He used it as a parable, not as history: it set real “Planck knowledge” against borrowed “chauffeur knowledge.”

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with an interchangeable star. Whoever is most famous for a hard subject gets the lead role, and Planck is just one of them.

items.why: Planck appears in Charlie Munger’s retelling, set in Munich, and Munger himself called it apocryphal ↗. The story does not appear on Planck’s Wikiquote page ↗.

Reader’s Digest ran an Einstein version in January 1978, crediting a West Virginia newspaper columnist, according to Quote Investigator ↗. Earlier printed versions named a rabbi or an unnamed scientist.
King Duncan’s Mule Eggs and Topknots (1987) cast the rocket scientist as the lecturer, as Quote Investigator ↗ documents.

Munger told the Planck version, in 2003 and 2007, but he presented it as an apocryphal “famous story.” Quote Investigator’s chronology has versions going back to 1926, decades before his talks (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The tale is anonymous Jewish folklore. Its earliest located version, from 1926, stars Rabbi Ezekiel Landau of Prague and his driver, and the scientists came later (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the Planck version stuck
lead: The Planck version spread because of what Munger built on it. In his 2007 USC commencement address he split knowledge into two kinds. “Planck knowledge” belongs to people who have paid their dues and really understand a subject. “Chauffeur knowledge” belongs to people who have “learned to prattle the talk” (Poor Charlie’s Almanack ↗). His fans repeated the parable, and Planck’s name went with it.

The joke itself is much older than the parable. In the 1926 version, the sharp-tongued stand-in is a rabbi’s driver, not a physicist’s chauffeur. The same punchline later passed through Einstein, von Braun and others before it reached Planck (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.pull: Chauffeur knowledge masquerading as real knowledge. — Charlie Munger, 2007

sourcesVerified.claim: QI traces the chauffeur anecdote to Jewish folklore. Its earliest match is Richman's 1926 Laughs from Jewish Lore, with Rabbi Ezekiel Landau, and the creator is unknown.

QI's chronology includes the Preacher of Dubno (1948), an unnamed atomic scientist (1958), Einstein (Reader's Digest, January 1978), von Braun (1987), a theologian (1998) and Munger's Planck version (2003, UCSB).

Richman's Laughs from Jewish Lore (Funk & Wagnalls, 1926) contains 'Even His Driver Was a Scholar' with Rabbi Ezekiel Landau and the line 'Even my driver can answer that'. Checked against the archive.org item's OCR text and metadata.

In his October 3, 2003 UCSB Herb Kay lecture, Munger calls the Planck story apocryphal and uses the wording 'so I'm going to ask my chauffeur to respond'. At USC on May 13, 2007, he says he frequently tells it and contrasts Planck knowledge with chauffeur knowledge.
Max Planck's Wikiquote page does not contain the chauffeur story. The raw page text has zero occurrences of 'chauffeur'.
Charlie Munger lived from 1924 to 2023 and was vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway.
